body.text: Fiji should aim to operate its Bluebottle surveillance boats jointly with Australia, not alone. The key independent capability that Fiji needs is not operation but tasking – deciding where the boats go, when they go and what they do on station.

Australian help in operating Fijian Bluebottles will get the greatest results from them. For example, operators who control and oversee Bluebottles’ work from desks in Australia can share shifts with those in Fiji, and Canberra can help with assessing what Fiji’s Bluebottles see.

Fiji will necessarily rely on Australian support to bring Fiji’s boats into service. They’re due for delivery in 2027. Canberra has promised training for Fijian operators and confirmed that the Bluebottles will belong to Fiji and operate under Fijian command.
Fiji would staff the watches that it wanted or needed to sustain independently. Australia could cover agreed shifts on other patrols for which Fiji could not readily fill the roster.

Developed in Australia, Bluebottles use solar, wind and wave energy to stay at sea for extended periods with no one aboard. In remarks reported on 30 October, Fijian Defence Minister Pio Tikoduadua emphasised the difficulty of watching Fiji’s vast waters and responding to suspicious activity – for example, activity of drug-running boats. Bluebottles can support this by patrolling, observing ships and boats, and sending their data ashore.

The success of joint operations was seen last year when Fiji and New Zealand worked together in watching waters around Fiji. On that occasion, the two Bluebottles belonged to New Zealand, whose operators worked alongside Republic of Fiji Navy personnel in Suva. A New Zealand team at Devonport covered the night watch. A New Zealand aircraft assisted in the operation.

The post-operation brief reported 41 days at sea for each Bluebottle and observation of 242 vessels – 100 of them not sending Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals. Although the absence of signal alone did not indicate wrongdoing, the joint effort was crucial because a watch relying on AIS broadcasts would have missed those vessels.

The deployment showed the Royal New Zealand Navy what staff it needed to operate prolonged watches from two locations. Fiji and Australia should use this as a model to share shifts on Fijian patrols. Canberra must decide whether to commit operators and funding regularly, so Suva can plan patrols around those shifts.

Another example of the value of joint operations occurred in a four-week deployment last month. At Fiji’s request, two New Zealand Bluebottles monitored known maritime routes around the clock to assess the volume and timing of traffic. The boats identified 137 vessels for further scrutiny by Fiji’s Maritime Essential Services Centre. The centre’s director, Lemeki Lenoa, then identified sustained observation as a priority and pointed to staffing and fuel costs as constraints.

Australia can help with the staffing, at least until the Fijian navy can build a sufficient workforce. Exercising mission command, officers in Fiji can determine Bluebottles’ movements, knowing that when Fijian operators go off shift, Australians will be standing by to take over. As it built up its workforce, Fiji might choose not to take over patrols entirely but to use ongoing availability of Australian operators to run more patrols.

The Royal Australian Navy, with deeper understanding of what Bluebottles can do, thanks to more extensive operations, can also lend advice to the Fijian navy on how to maximise effectiveness of the boats. When RAN operators were used, the passing of advice might be a routine, day-to-day process: as they handed over to the next shift, the Australians could let the Fijians know how they had dealt with issues that had come up.

The resources and expertise available to the RAN can also be used to help assess surveillance data that Fijian Bluebottles collected. Australia may also be able to send an aircraft or ship to check out a suspicious contact.
All this should be part of the Pacific Maritime Security Program, through which Australia already helps partners maintain patrol boats and train crews.

In announcing the intended supply of Bluebottles to Fiji, Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy pointed to the problem of drugs being smuggled through the Pacific to Australia. This highlighted a mutual priority for the two countries in sustaining patrols. So Australia has a direct interest in getting the most out of Fijian Bluebottle patrols.
Fijian operators could also join RAN watches for practice – learning, for example, how to keep a patrol running through an equipment fault.

In helping the Fijian navy to operate Bluebottles, the RAN would also gain an understanding of its partner’s abilities. It may eventually be pleased to pass Australian tasking to Fijian boats, or even call on Fijian operators to help run Australian Bluebottles in a busy period.

Joint operation of Fiji’s Bluebottles would make the country’s patrols more effective, strengthen its ocean-watch capacity and build an interdependent monitoring scheme that would benefit both countries.
